I used to live in Chicago in the 80s and 90s, and actually new Morningstar when it was very

And in fact, it's just a coincidence, but their focus on the first dovetails
with what I've always thought are important and fundamental
aspects of investing. Anyway, the subject at hand today, which I'm going to talk about is
the Ten Commandments of Investment Management. And these commandments basically evolved over the years
years and actually I came up with the framework in the last few months. But they've been very fundamental
and I don't think they're really subject to debate, if you will. It's almost like the laws of
physics. So given that we're on a somewhat tight schedule, I'll get going with them.
The first commandment, which is thou shall not skim off the top.
And just in case that's nebulous, when Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger ran their investment partnerships in the 1950s and 60s, the fee structure that Buffett followed was to not charge any management fees.
There was zero management fees.
And then there was a 6% hurdle, and then he got paid one-fourth of the returns above 6% and was subject to high watermark.
For example, if the fund was up 10% in a year, he would get paid 1%.
If it was up 5%, he wouldn't get paid anything.
And if he was up 15%, he would get about 2.5%.
So it was a complete alignment with the investors.
And the fee structure has a number of effects on how fund managers think.
So one of the first effects it has is that they stop becoming asset gathering machines
because you don't get paid for assets, you get paid for performance.
And that's generally a good thing.
And the second is that they get focused on trying to do the best investing they can, and it would lead
to a lot of other things, for example, being relatively concentrated.
The lack of fees also means the lack of a team, which I will get to in the second commandment.
But basically there's intense focus that comes out of that on not having frivolous
expenses. So the question that a lot of investment managers would have
is well, how do I take care of the expenses of an investment operation if I'm not guaranteed
a certain amount of fees? My answer to that is that if you set up a steel mill or you start
an airline or almost any other business venture set up a refinery, there is nothing
ordained in capitalism that assures you that those ventures would make money.
It's a risk. And so investment management also, if you set up an operation and you, now this is relatively
low cap-ex, but if you set up an operation, you have some expenses, that's fine. If you do well,
the operation will end up being successful. If you don't do well, then it doesn't deserve
to keep off the top and cover some of the losses. It works out.
Now, the second commandment which actually dovetails in the first one,
is thou shall not have an investing team.
And this is something that always puzzles and surprises me is when I look at Warren Buffett and
and Charlie Munger again, so today Buffett is managing, I think, something north of 400 billion
in assets. I think the stock portfolio of cash investments is about north of
$200 billion. And there's no team. He doesn't have an analyst. He doesn't
have any associates. He manages that by himself. And besides managing the
$200 billion of investments, on the side, he, until recently, also managed about 80 CEOs and businesses
that are producing $10, $20 billion a year in cash flows. So not only is he a leader of a large
conglomerate with lots of direct reports, he has a very significant portfolio. And on the other
hand, I routinely run into funds that would have maybe under a hundred
crores or 200 crores of assets with several people hovering around. And I actually don't understand
what they do because basically you need to find about three or four stocks in a year. And I don't
know why you need even more than half a human to do that. But the industry works a certain
way and it doesn't work the way, the high priests of the industry and the gods of
investing have said that it should work. And actually, when you follow the
first commandment, which is not skimming off the top, it actually automatically leads to following the second
commandment. Because if you're not going to be collecting fees on a certain amount of assets, you'd be
really careful about how the money is being spent. So I routinely see investment
operations with a lot of fat and a lot of misuse of the management fees.
They go to areas which really have nothing to do with delivering performance. And going on to
Commandment 3, I'm going to move along on these in a little fast pace because we've got to get through
all 10 of these and then have some time for Q&A. But the third one is at least one third
of the time. And so this comes from John Templeton. If we are going to try to figure
out the future of a business, what a business looks like five years from
now or 10 years from now. By definition, that type of an endeavor is going to have a very high error
because there are lots of uncertainties that come in when we look at long-term futures
of businesses. And even the best investment manager, John Templeton introduced to say,
even the best investment analyst, will be wrong at least one out of three times.
Now, when they're wrong, it doesn't mean that they lose money.
It could be that you thought, oh, this stock is going to triple and it flatline.
Or maybe it goes down 10%. Or it maybe goes up 50%. But it doesn't do what you expected it to do.
And the good news with the investment business is that even with a very healthy error rate, even if you're

if you're a brain surgeon, you cannot have a 40% error rate or
a 4% error rate or even a 0.4% error rate doesn't work. But the investing
business is a very forgiving business, and it tolerates a high error rate, which is great. The next one,
now shall look for hidden P.E.O1 stocks. And just so there's no confusion, P.O1 means that the company
in the next one year earns what the market cap is, which is generally good for your
financial health. There's, let's say, around 50,000 publicly traded stocks on
the planet. And let's say I run a screen which says, I only want to look at stocks
that have a multiple of 40 or less. Probably tens of thousands of thousands of companies will fit that.
And then if you keep tightening the news to saying, I won't be of 30 or less or 20 or less,
that number is going to keep going down. But in an auction-driven market, which most all stock
stock market is auction-driven market, it is the norm that we get wide mispricing.
And every so often, we get mispricing, which is very much in our favor as buyers.
Sometimes it's in our favor as sellers where things get very euphoric.
So generally, when things get very pessimistic, we want to be buying, and when things get very
